_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-05 01:21:14Z)**_

Replies are now a few plain sentences with the map doing the explaining, and Claude no longer writes the longer versions at all. All 136 tests pass (including a new one), typecheck and build are clean, and in the preview a reply now shows only its short answer.

**What Claude is asked to write now**
- **Answers:** just the plain answer, 2–4 sentences. When it lights up the map, it should say what the lit path shows instead of walking through every step, and name a function or file only when you asked about the code and it isn't on the map. The step-by-step and code-reference versions are gone from what Claude is asked for, so it can't spend time on them.
- **Boxes:** the map maker writes only a 1–2 sentence explanation per box and leaves out function and file names, since the box already shows them. That cuts a large share of the writing when making a map, so new maps should come back faster.

**The two side issues** (both are new instructions to Claude):
- It's told to explain the code and the app, not its own instructions.
- It's told to only add to the map when what it found belongs to the flow the map follows and seeing it drawn helps answer the question. Otherwise it answers in words.

These have only been run against the scripted Claude, never the real one. They should help with things like "Added 5 to the map" on a question about the screen, but the routing eval we discussed is how you'd confirm it.

**What stays the same**
- The map format: boxes can still carry the longer fields, so older saved maps load. Those fields just aren't shown.
- Code on the map: every box still shows its function and file, and clicking one still shows the checked lines under "In the code".

The changes are in `prompts.ts`, `schemas.ts`, `explainer.ts` and `server.ts` on the server, and `panel.tsx`, `state.ts` and `styles.css` in the viewer. I updated the README and CLAUDE.md. HANDOFF lists "three depths" as interviewee feedback, so I left that line and added a dated note saying they were dropped and why.

Reload your tab to see it. Nothing is committed yet.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-05 01:39:58Z)**_

Claude Code shows Claude's replies as Markdown, the formatting syntax used in GitHub READMEs. Claude writes `**bold**`, `` `code` ``, `- ` bullets, headings and blank lines between paragraphs, and the terminal turns those into structure. That's why replies there look broken up.

Illuminate does it differently, for two reasons:

1. **It's on purpose.** The answer comes back as one text field in a fixed structure, and the instructions now ask for 2–4 plain sentences. That's a single paragraph almost by definition.
2. **The viewer shows that text as plain text.** It keeps line breaks, but it doesn't interpret any formatting. You could see this in the reply you pasted earlier: `**Read the reply.**` and the backticks around `` `current` `` came through as raw symbols. Claude writes Markdown out of habit, and we show it literally.

**Do you need more?** Not with the new short answers. Their job is to say what's lit on the map, and one paragraph suits that. Longer formatted answers are what we just removed.

**If you want a bit of polish anyway**, there are two small options:
- **Tell Claude plain text only:** no Markdown symbols. Then it never shows raw `**` or backticks. It's one line in the prompt.
- **Show a small subset properly:** paragraph breaks, **bold**, `code` and short lists. I'd write a tiny converter for just those, rather than add a library that renders arbitrary Markdown. This is safer and keeps the answer readable if Claude does list a few steps.

My suggestion is the first, since it matches "short, plain, the map explains". Want me to add it?

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-05 01:41:18Z)**_

Adding a small converter in the viewer that turns Claude's Markdown into real formatting: paragraphs, line breaks, **bold**, *italics*, `code`, code blocks, bullet and numbered lists, headings and links. It builds the page elements directly instead of injecting HTML, so nothing Claude writes can run as code on the page. I'll use it everywhere Claude writes prose: replies, box explanations, walkthrough stops and fix summaries.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-05 01:41:34Z)**_

<tool-use data-tool-type="write" data-tool-name="Write"><details>
<summary>Tool use: **Write**</summary>

````typescript
// Claude writes Markdown out of habit; show it as formatting rather than symbols. A small, safe subset: paragraphs and
// line breaks, headings, bullet and numbered lists, code blocks, **bold**, *italic*, `code` and [links](https://…).
// It builds React elements (never HTML strings), so nothing in the text can run on the page.
import type { ReactNode } from 'react';

type Block =
  | { kind: 'p'; text: string }
  | { kind: 'h'; text: string }
  | { kind: 'ul'; items: string[] }
  | { kind: 'ol'; items: string[]; start: number }
  | { kind: 'code'; text: string };

const FENCE = /^\s*(```|~~~)/;
const HEADING = /^\s{0,3}#{1,6}\s+(.*?)\s*#*\s*$/;
const BULLET = /^\s*[-*+•]\s+(.*)$/;
const NUMBERED = /^\s*(\d{1,4})[.)]\s+(.*)$/;

/** Splits text into blocks: a blank line ends a paragraph; list items and code fences are their own blocks. */
export function parseBlocks(src: string): Block[] {
  const lines = src.replace(/\r\n?/g, '\n').split('\n');
  const blocks: Block[] = [];
  let para: string[] = [];
  const flush = () => {
    if (para.length) blocks.push({ kind: 'p', text: para.join('\n') });
    para = [];
  };
  for (let i = 0; i < lines.length; i++) {
    const line = lines[i]!;
    if (FENCE.test(line)) {
      flush();
      const body: string[] = [];
      for (i++; i < lines.length && !FENCE.test(lines[i]!); i++) body.push(lines[i]!);
      blocks.push({ kind: 'code', text: body.join('\n') });
      continue;
    }
    if (!line.trim()) {
      flush();
      continue;
    }
    const h = HEADING.exec(line);
    if (h) {
      flush();
      blocks.push({ kind: 'h', text: h[1]! });
      continue;
    }
    const b = BULLET.exec(line);
    const n = b ? null : NUMBERED.exec(line);
    if (b || n) {
      flush();
      const kind = b ? 'ul' : 'ol';
      const last = blocks[blocks.length - 1];
      const item = b ? b[1]! : n![2]!;
      if (last && last.kind === kind) last.items.push(item);
      else blocks.push(kind === 'ul' ? { kind, items: [item] } : { kind, items: [item], start: Number(n![1]) });
      continue;
    }
    // A line that carries on a list item (indented, right after it) belongs to that item.
    const last = blocks[blocks.length - 1];
    if (!para.length && last && (last.kind === 'ul' || last.kind === 'ol') && /^\s+\S/.test(line)) {
      last.items[last.items.length - 1] += ` ${line.trim()}`;
      continue;
    }
    para.push(line);
  }
  flush();
  return blocks;
}

// `code`, **bold** / __bold__, *italic* / _italic_ (not inside words, so snake_case stays), [text](url).
const INLINE = /(`+)([^`]+?)\1|\*\*(.+?)\*\*|__(.+?)__|\*(?!\s)(.+?)\*|(?<![\w])_(?!\s)(.+?)_(?![\w])|\[([^\]]+)\]\(([^)\s]+)\)/g;

/** Inline formatting within a block. Single line breaks stay line breaks. */
export function inline(text: string, key = 'i'): ReactNode[] {
  const out: ReactNode[] = [];
  let at = 0;
  let n = 0;
  const plain = (s: string) => {
    s.split('\n').forEach((part, i) => {
      if (i > 0) out.push(<br key={`${key}-br${n++}`} />);
      if (part) out.push(part);
    });
  };
  for (const m of text.matchAll(INLINE)) {
    plain(text.slice(at, m.index));
    const k = `${key}-${n++}`;
    if (m[2] !== undefined) out.push(<code key={k}>{m[2]}</code>);
    else if (m[3] !== undefined || m[4] !== undefined) out.push(<strong key={k}>{inline(m[3] ?? m[4]!, k)}</strong>);
    else if (m[5] !== undefined || m[6] !== undefined) out.push(<em key={k}>{inline(m[5] ?? m[6]!, k)}</em>);
    else if (m[7] !== undefined) {
      const url = m[8]!;
      // Only real web links open; anything else (a file path, javascript:) stays as text.
      out.push(/^https?:\/\//i.test(url) ? <a key={k} href={url} target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">{inline(m[7], k)}</a> : <span key={k}>{inline(m[7], k)}</span>);
    }
    at = m.index + m[0].length;
  }
  plain(text.slice(at));
  return out;
}

export function Markdown({ text, className }: { text: string; className?: string }) {
  const blocks = parseBlocks(text);
  if (!blocks.length) return null;
  return (
    <div className={className ? `md ${className}` : 'md'}>
      {blocks.map((b, i) => {
        const k = `b${i}`;
        if (b.kind === 'p') return <p key={k}>{inline(b.text, k)}</p>;
        if (b.kind === 'h') return <p key={k} className="md-h">{inline(b.text, k)}</p>;
        if (b.kind === 'code') return <pre key={k}><code>{b.text}</code></pre>;
        const items = b.items.map((it, j) => <li key={`${k}-${j}`}>{inline(it, `${k}-${j}`)}</li>);
        return b.kind === 'ul' ? <ul key={k}>{items}</ul> : <ol key={k} start={b.start}>{items}</ol>;
      })}
    </div>
  );
}

};

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-05 04:12:35Z)**_

**How the number is made.** Nothing about it is stored. Each time the map is shown, the checker (`check()` in `packages/core/src/check.ts`) re-reads your repo as it is right now and re-tests every claim on the map. It's plain code, with no call to Claude, so it's fast and gives the same result every time. There are three kinds of claim:

- **Boxes:** each box cites a line of code, such as `bus.emit('patient.converted'…` at `service.ts:6`. The checker opens that file and looks for that text on that line. It also accepts the text up to 3 lines away (`lineWindow`), so small edits elsewhere in the file don't break it. If the box names a function, the function must still exist.
- **Arrows:** a "calls" arrow must be a real call from one function to the other in the code. "request" and "imports" arrows are checked the same way against the code's actual requests and imports. Other arrows just need their cited line to still say what it said.
- **Gaps** ("nothing listens for X"): the checker re-runs the exact search behind the claim and checks it still finds the same number of matches, usually zero. If someone has since added a listener, the gap stops checking out.

"44 of 50" means 6 of those tests failed against today's code.

**When it runs:**
- when you open or reload a map,
- after every answer,
- after a fix is applied or undone,
- and from the terminal with `illume check <map-id>`, which exits with an error if anything fails, so it could run in CI.

It doesn't watch your files. If you edit code while a map is open, the count only updates on the next reload or answer.

**How a map goes out of date.** Its claims were tested against the code as it was when it was made. In your case, this repo has changed a lot since some of those maps were drawn: we renamed codemap to illuminate and rewrote the panel. Lines that cited `bin/codemap.mjs` or the old tabs no longer exist where the map says, so those claims fail. That's what the number is for: telling you the map no longer matches the code.

**Seeing which ones.** Failed claims are drawn dashed with a "?" on the map. Click one and the panel says why, for example "Couldn't confirm against the code: line 52 no longer says …".

So the counter itself is just a summary. If you remove it, nothing important goes missing as long as the "?" marks stay. A possible middle ground: show nothing while everything checks out, and show a plain line only when it doesn't, such as "6 parts of this map no longer match the code". Say which you want.

**Three of the four aren't buyers.**

Shonn plans the design himself and checks by running the app. Abel has his own setup of agents that write specs. People like this will never feel the pain, however good the tool is. That's useful to know, but it doesn't count against the idea.

**The contractor is the one real signal, for three reasons:**
1. **He has a clear trigger.** A client asks for a change, and he has to understand the system before he can make it.
2. **He has a reason not to hand it to Claude.** He doesn't trust it, and he comes from security.
3. **He already does something about it.** He showed you his Claude chat asking how the KPIs were sourced. Asking Claude in chat is the thing illuminate has to beat.

**How to describe the audience.** It isn't "people who care about the codebase." It's people who have to change, or answer for, a system they don't fully hold. That covers a contractor taking a client's change request, someone inheriting a codebase, and the PM asked to explain Waymo's backend. It also covers your original EHR story.

**You're right about frontend plus backend, with one change.** Look at where both strong stories start:
- The EHR story: "I just trusted what I saw on the frontend."
- The contractor: "press on the KPI and see what feeds it."

Both start from something on screen, not from a typed question. So I wouldn't build the journey view as a second product next to the backend map. I'd make the screen the way into it: click a component, and the checked backend map unfolds behind it. Your note from yesterday already pointed this way ("behind this tap" keeps the backend map underneath). The interviews tell you to make that the entry point, not a later add-on.

**This is cheaper to test than it sounds.** Tracing a screen component through its fetch, the API route, the query and down to the data source is mostly what the maker and checker already do. The checker already verifies request and call arrows. The new part is starting from the UI instead of a question.

**Two cautions:**
- It's one strong interview out of four. Don't rebuild around it until a second person in the same situation reacts the same way.
- What people say they'd want isn't what they'd use. The real test is whether a map beats asking Claude in chat.

**My suggestion:** go back to the contractor with one of his real dashboards, or a repo shaped like it. Make the map for "where does this KPI come from?", starting from the component, and watch whether he trusts it more than his chat answer. If he does, the frontend entry point is worth building. If he shrugs, the problem is real but the map isn't the answer, and that's worth learning before more viewer work.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-05 22:24:37Z)**_

I think part of illuminate's pitch is temporary and part of it gets stronger as models improve. It's worth separating the two now.

**What probably goes away:** worry about the code itself. Overengineering, messy structure, the agent "bullshitting" its way to code that technically works. Models will get much better at all of that. If illuminate's pitch is "catch bad engineering," it shrinks as models improve. Shonn is partly right there.

**What doesn't go away:** knowing what your system actually does. Better models make that harder, because more of the system gets written that no person has read. A perfect codebase is only perfect against some intent, and the intent lives with people. The contractor's point about edge cases isn't about model skill. It's that Claude doesn't know what his client meant, what's legally risky, or what "converted" means in their business. Your EHR story wasn't badly engineered code either. Something that should have been connected wasn't, and the frontend gave no hint.

Compilers are a useful comparison. They got essentially perfect, and nobody reads assembly any more. People didn't stop needing to understand their programs; they moved up a level. Tests, monitoring, and code review that's about intent rather than syntax all exist because "the machine did it right" and "it does what I meant" are different questions. As people read less code, the need for checked explanations of behaviour grows.

**That suggests where to aim:**
- **Not:** "Is this code well engineered?" That fades.
- **Yes:** "What happens when X? What feeds this number? Does anything actually handle this?" That lasts. The checker matters more here: an explanation verified against the repo is worth more when nobody wrote the code by hand. Gaps ("nothing listens for this") are the clearest case, because a silent failure is exactly what testing by hand misses.

**The real long-term risks are different ones:**
1. **Testing by using the app may be enough for most people.** That's what Shonn does. A map only wins when you need to understand before you change or run something, or when the failure is silent. That may be a narrower group, though it's the one you found: contractors, regulated domains like EHR, people inheriting code.
2. **It could become a feature of something bigger.** Claude Code, or an IDE, could add diagrams. If that happens, the diagram isn't what keeps people. What's left is verification, and the screen-to-wiring entry point, if you've made those really good.

**My view:** observability of what a system does is a durable need, and it grows as people write less of the code themselves. Code quality as a pitch isn't durable. Whether illuminate is a company or a feature is a separate, open question, and that's the one worth testing.

The contractor test I suggested checks both at once. Does he trust a checked map over Claude's chat answer, and does he need it before he makes the change?

Yes, almost. I'd sharpen it, though, because "visual vs chat" is the wrong axis. A Mermaid diagram in chat is visual too. What separates illuminate from chat plus Mermaid is mostly not the picture.

| | Claude chat + Mermaid | Testing the app | illuminate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shows the wiring | Yes | No, only the results | Yes |
| Claims are checked against the code | No, an arrow can be made up | n/a | Yes |
| Shows what's *missing* ("nothing listens for this") | Only if Claude happens to notice | Only if you happen to trigger it | Yes, and the search that proves it is re-run |
| Still true next week | No, it's a one-off snapshot | You have to re-test | Re-checked every time it opens |
| You can point at a part and ask | Awkward | No | Yes |

So the real question is: **does checked, lasting and pointable beat good enough and already there?**

For many questions chat wins. It costs nothing, it's where people already are, and it's usually right. illuminate only wins when at least one of these holds:
- **A wrong answer is costly.** The contractor about to make a client's change, or anything in EHR.
- **The failure is silent.** Testing won't show it, and chat won't think to mention it.
- **You come back to the same system repeatedly.** A map that stays true beats re-asking.
- **The system is too big for one chat answer to hold.**

If those moments are rare for your users, chat is enough and illuminate is a nice-to-have.

**We can test this ourselves before asking anyone.** The care-app fixture has a planted gap: no welcome email is sent after a patient converts. Run it against plain Claude Code, ask "what happens when a patient converts? Draw it as a Mermaid diagram," and see:
